_comment: Guided tour for the FCS curve merger. The page is a .ui-loaded QWizardPage, so steps target widgets by objectName -- lineEdit (the folder), tableWidget (the per-curve Use column), toolButton_3 (save the merged curve). There is no view spec. Read by chisurf.gui.widgets.tools.guided_tour.

steps.title: The averaging is arithmetic — the choosing is the work
steps.text:
A single short FCS acquisition is noisy exactly where the information is: at short lag, where few photon pairs contribute. Many short runs plus a merge gets the statistics without the photobleaching and drift of one long run.

And it gives you something a long run cannot — the chance to look at the repeats and throw away the ones that went wrong. That is what this window is for; the averaging itself is a mean.

Five steps.

steps.title: Point it at the correlation folder
steps.text: Drop a folder of correlation files here, or browse to one. Every curve it finds is loaded, plotted and listed.

await.hint: Choose or drop the folder holding your correlation curves.

steps.title: The table is the screening tool, not a file list
steps.text:
Each row carries the two count rates and the duration alongside the file, because those are what tell you whether two curves are measurements of the same thing.

They matter because averaging assumes exactly that. G(0) = 1/N, so averaging curves taken at different concentrations gives a mean amplitude that is the mean of the reciprocals — not a concentration you can quote. A focus that drifted between runs changes τ_D too, so the merged decay is broader than anything in the sample.

Untick a row to leave it out; double-click toggles it.

steps.title: One aggregate can move the whole mean
steps.text:
This is why the checkboxes exist. A single bright particle crossing the focus adds a large, slow contribution — and because G is normalised by the square of the mean intensity, one such event can dominate an entire curve.

On the left plot it is unmistakable once you know it: an amplitude sitting above the family, and a shoulder at long lag the others do not have. Unticked curves are drawn dashed and grey, so you can compare before and after without losing them.

Averaging that curve in does not dilute it. It moves the mean.

Also leave out the first curve of a session (often taken before the temperature settled) and anything whose shape is qualitatively different rather than merely noisier — noise averages down, a different shape does not.

steps.title: Save it, then ask four questions
steps.text:
The right plot is the merge of the ticked curves; saving writes it out, and it can be added to ChiSurf as an FCS dataset ready to fit.

Before it becomes a number in a figure:
1. Do the ticked curves agree in amplitude? If not they are not the same concentration, and the merged G(0) means nothing.
2. Do they agree in shape? Overlap is what merging assumes; scatter is what it fixes.
3. How many survived? A mean of three is a mean of three however smooth it looks — the noise improves as √n and no faster.
4. Would the conclusion change if you unticked the most extreme curve? If so, it rests on that curve rather than on the merge.

The ? button has the rest.

await.hint: Press the save button to write the merged curve.
